subject: business
title: Jobs to Be Done: hire the product for the progress the buyer is trying to make
dek: Clayton Christensen, Scott Cook, and Taddy Hall’s December 2005 Harvard Business Review essay, and the September 2016 follow-up with Karen Dillon and David S. Duncan: stop segmenting by demographics or product category. Ask what job customers hire the offer to do. The milkshake commute study, Southern New Hampshire University’s online rebuild, and IKEA’s “furnish it now” integration are the cases — only for facts named public pages actually state.

hero.caption: A McDonald’s strawberry milkshake, 14 April 2022. The December 2005 Harvard Business Review essay disguised the chain; Christensen later told the milkshake story with McDonald’s named. The object here is the product category the morning-commute research was about — thick, one-handed, slow to finish — not a claim that this cup was the redesigned morning SKU.

honesty: This is a strategy-framework lesson, not a company biography and not a promise that naming a “job” always raises sales. The December 2005 HBR essay (“Marketing Malpractice”) disguises the fast-food chain; Harvard Business School Working Knowledge (14 February 2011) and Christensen’s later talks name McDonald’s. Claims about what morning buyers said (boring commute, one free hand, hunger by mid-morning, 40 percent of shakes bought early) are taken from that Working Knowledge piece and from Christensen’s public retellings, not from invented store data. The essay and the 2011 piece do not publish a before-and-after sales chart for a redesigned morning shake, so this capsule does not invent one. Southern New Hampshire University’s use of jobs language is taken from Competing Against Luck authors’ public accounts (Boston Globe, 4 October 2016) and from later named reporting; operating statistics those pages do not state are omitted. IKEA is Christensen’s example of a firm hard to copy because it integrates around a job (“furnish an apartment right now”), not a claim that IKEA’s founders used the 2005 vocabulary. Theodore Levitt’s Marketing Myopia (1960) is named as an earlier hole-not-drill framing, not as identical theory. Tony Ulwick’s outcome-driven work is named where priority fights over credit appear in public discussion; this lesson does not adjudicate patents. “Blue ocean” from the earlier Saturday capsule is named only where noncustomers and reconstructed offers overlap; Southwest is not reused.

fun_fact.title: The 2005 essay hid the restaurant; the podcast did not
fun_fact.text: In “Marketing Malpractice,” the milkshake chain is anonymous. By the December 2016 HBR Ideacast, Christensen says “McDonald’s” out loud when he retells the commute study. The method is the same; the brand label in public talk is not. Treat the cup in this lesson as the category under study, not as a stamped proof that HBR’s disguised chain was already named in print in 2005.

glossary.explain: Christensen and colleagues’ name for understanding a purchase as hiring a product to make progress in a specific circumstance. Public HBR statements: December 2005 (“Marketing Malpractice”) and September 2016 (“Know Your Customers’ ‘Jobs to Be Done’”).
In this theory: the progress a customer seeks in a particular circumstance — functional, social, and emotional. Not a job title and not a product category.
Jobs vocabulary for choosing a product to get a job done. If it works, the customer tends to hire it again; if not, they fire it.
Jobs vocabulary for dropping a product that did a crummy job and looking for an alternative.
The situation in which the job arises — time of day, constraints, what else is available — which the 2016 essay treats as more critical than buyer demographics.

sections.title: When you know the buyer’s age and still miss why they buy

blocks.text: Most marketing systems can describe a customer. They know an age band, an income band, a preferred channel, a past basket. The December 2005 Harvard Business Review essay “Marketing Malpractice: The Cause and the Cure,” by Clayton M. Christensen, Scott Cook, and Taddy Hall, opens on a blunt failure rate: tens of thousands of new consumer products launch each year, and most of them do not stick — after firms have already spent heavily to “understand” what buyers want. The authors’ claim is not that researchers are stupid. It is that the usual ways of cutting a market — by product category, or by demographic profile — organize data that is easy to collect and still miss the cause of a purchase.

The open page of that essay quotes A.G. Lafley, then CEO of Procter & Gamble, saying marketing needs a new model. Christensen’s later teaching line, recorded in Carmen Nobel’s 14 February 2011 Harvard Business School Working Knowledge piece, is sharper: being eighteen to thirty-five with a college degree does not cause you to buy a product. It may correlate with the decision. The causal mechanism, in this view, is that a job has arisen in someone’s life, and they hire something to get it done.

blocks.alt: Clayton Christensen seated on a stage interview set beside Economist editor Zanny Minton Beddoes, World Economic Forum session.
blocks.caption: Clayton Christensen with Zanny Minton Beddoes at a World Economic Forum “An insight, An Idea” session. Christensen is the public voice of jobs-to-be-done in the sources this lesson uses. The still is a portrait of the teacher, not a chart of milkshake sales.
blocks.credit: World Economic Forum / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0

blocks.text: Theodore Levitt had already warned, in “Marketing Myopia” (Harvard Business Review, 1960), that firms which define themselves by the product they make can miss the need they serve. The quarter-inch drill bit is famous because people want the hole. Jobs to Be Done keeps that pressure and adds method: watch the circumstance, name the progress, and treat bagels, bananas, and boredom as real competitors when that is what the buyer is choosing among.

sections.title: Progress in a circumstance — hire, fire, and the dimensions of a job

blocks.text: A job, in the September 2016 HBR essay by Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, and David S. Duncan, is the progress a customer seeks in a particular circumstance. Some jobs are small (pass the time in a line). Some are large (find a more fulfilling career). Some arrive on a schedule (pack a lunch). Some arrive because a suitcase was lost. When someone buys, they hire a product to help. If it does the job well, they tend to hire it again. If it does a crummy job, they fire it and look for something else.

Three commitments sit inside that sentence. First, circumstance beats persona: the same person hires different things at 7 a.m. on a commute and at 7 p.m. with a child. Second, a job is not only functional. The 2016 essay insists on social and emotional dimensions — how the choice makes someone feel, and how it looks to others — as load-bearing, not decorative. Third, the set of candidates for hire is wider than the shelf category. A morning milkshake competes with a bagel that crumbs on a shirt, a banana that is gone too fast, and the empty boredom of the drive.

The 2016 essay also places jobs theory beside Christensen’s earlier disruptive-innovation work. Disruption theory, the authors write, explains how incumbents respond when entrants attack; it does not, by itself, tell you what to build that customers will hire. Jobs theory is offered as that missing causal story of choice. You do not need to accept every later consulting worksheet to use the core move: stop asking only who the buyer is, and ask what progress they are trying to make, under what constraints, with what else on offer.

Purpose branding, in the 2011 Working Knowledge piece, is one organizational consequence. Kodak’s FunSaver names the job of preserving a fun occasion. Milwaukee’s Sawzall names the job of cutting through almost anything. The company name alone, Christensen argues there, does not give you the market. The job name can. That is a branding claim, not a guarantee — and it is why the theory keeps returning to verbs of progress rather than nouns of category.

sections.title: A commute shake, an online university, and a store built around “now”

people.name: Clayton M. Christensen
people.text: Co-author of the December 2005 and September 2016 HBR jobs essays and of Competing Against Luck. Public voice of the milkshake study and of jobs theory as a complement to disruptive innovation.

people.name: Scott Cook
people.text: Co-founder of Intuit; co-author of “Marketing Malpractice” (HBR, December 2005). Ties the framework to a product company without requiring a fabricated release note.

people.name: Taddy Hall
people.text: Co-author of both HBR jobs essays and of Competing Against Luck.

people.name: Karen Dillon
people.text: Former HBR editor; co-author of the September 2016 essay and of Competing Against Luck.

people.name: David S. Duncan
people.text: Co-author of the September 2016 essay and of Competing Against Luck.

people.name: Paul LeBlanc
people.text: Named in the authors’ public SNHU accounts as the leader who separated “coming of age” from “step it up” and rebuilt online adult processes around the second job.

blocks.text: The milkshake study is the teaching case that made the method audible. A fast-food chain wanted more shake sales. It segmented by product and by the demographic of a “typical” shake buyer, asked that profile what an ideal shake was like, and improved along those answers. Sales did not move. A researcher then spent a day watching who bought shakes, when, and whether they drank them in the restaurant. About 40 percent were bought first thing in the morning, to go. The next morning’s interviews, as Nobel reports Christensen’s account, found a shared job: a long, boring commute; at most one free hand; work clothes; not hungry yet but hungry by mid-morning. The thick shake through a thin straw lasted, stayed tidy, and gave the drive something to do. Bagels and doughnuts failed parts of that job. Once the job was named, the improvement list changed — thicker for the morning, more interesting with fruit chunks, faster to buy — and a different, thinner shake for the afternoon “treat for a child” job, where a half-hour struggle with a straw punished the parent.

blocks.alt: McDonald’s strawberry milkshake in a clear cup with whipped topping and a red straw.
blocks.caption: The category under study. The 2005 essay kept the chain anonymous; later talks named McDonald’s. This 2022 cup is evidence of the product type, not a before-and-after sales chart. The HBS write-up does not publish a proprietary lift number for a redesigned morning SKU, so this lesson does not invent one.
blocks.credit: Dr Salvus / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Southern New Hampshire University is the case of a firm that used the language to rebuild an offer, not only to tell a classroom story. Paul LeBlanc became president in 2003. In the authors’ Boston Globe excerpt (4 October 2016) and in Competing Against Luck’s public retellings, SNHU was serving at least two different jobs with one institutional habit. Traditional-age undergraduates often hired residential college for a “coming of age” job — campus life, clubs, the transition into adulthood. Working adults hiring the online programs needed something else: to “step it up” in a career while raising children or holding a job. Prestige theater and climbing walls were the wrong improvements for that second job. Speed of financial aid, convenience, personal advising, and fewer administrative hurdles were the right ones. The strategic content is the separation of jobs and the redesign of processes around the adult online hire — not a claim that every enrollment chart in later press can be pasted here without its own source line.

blocks.alt: Entrance to Southern New Hampshire University’s College of Online and Continuing Education building.
blocks.caption: Entrance to SNHU’s College of Online and Continuing Education (COCE), photographed by Steve Lux, Jr. The building stands for the online adult channel the jobs accounts describe — the “step it up” hire — not for a full campus tour.
blocks.credit: Steve Lux, Jr. / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: IKEA, in Christensen’s 2011 Working Knowledge remarks, is the integration exhibit. Nobody, he says there, has managed to copy IKEA, which helps customers do the job of furnishing an apartment right now. The point is not a single low-price sofa. It is the stack that serves the job: showroom path, flat packs in the warehouse aisle, tools and bits in the same trip, food for the family that came along, childcare in some stores. A rival can match a SKU and still fail the job if the afternoon still requires four other shops. That is why jobs theory talks about organizing around the job, not only about writing a better feature list inside an old org chart.

blocks.alt: Self-serve warehouse aisle at IKEA Torp in Uddevalla, Sweden, with flat-pack shelves rising on both sides.
blocks.caption: Self-serve aisle, IKEA Torp, Uddevalla, Sweden. The flat-pack run is part of the “furnish it now” stack Christensen points to — warehouse picking in the same visit as the showroom — not a claim that this Swedish store was designed from the 2005 HBR vocabulary.

blocks.alt: Scott Cook of Intuit speaking on stage at SXSW 2017.
blocks.caption: Scott Cook of Intuit at SXSW 2017. Cook co-authored the December 2005 HBR essay. His name ties the framework to a product company; this lesson does not invent a Quicken release note from that fact alone.

sections.title: Other morning hires: the konbini commute

blocks.text: The milkshake problem is a morning-progress problem. In Japan, in the same decades the HBR essays were circulating, Lawson, FamilyMart, and 7-Eleven stores were already dense along station approaches — hot cans, onigiri, coffee machines, a layout built for a one-handed walk to the platform. That is not “Asia’s version of McDonald’s.” It is a contemporaneous retail form hired for a related job: get something tidy, fast, and filling enough into a commuting body without sitting down. The jobs lens travels; the SKU list does not have to.

blocks.alt: Lawson convenience store front on a Tokyo street in Nishi-Ikebukuro, March 2007.
blocks.caption: Lawson, Nishi-Ikebukuro, Tokyo, 2 March 2007. A station-neighborhood konbini is a morning hire for many Tokyo commuters. Place it next to the milkshake study as a parallel circumstance — hurry, one hand, work clothes — not as a licensed Christensen exhibit.

blocks.alt: Wide interior view of a FamilyMart store in Chatan, Okinawa, showing aisles and refrigerated cases.
blocks.caption: FamilyMart interior, Chatan Fisherina, Okinawa. The open refrigerated run and grab-and-go layout are how a different chain serves the same class of job: progress before the next obligation, without a table service script.
blocks.credit: Nelo Hotsuma / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0

blocks.text: Elsewhere in the same years, online degree programs and open universities were also sorting “coming of age” from “step it up,” whether or not they used Christensen’s nouns. The SNHU story matters because its leaders and the book authors said the jobs words out loud and redesigned processes to match. Other systems can land on the same separation by another route. Contemporaneous does not mean copied.

sections.title: A useful causal story is still easy to fake

blocks.text: Jobs language can become a slogan. Any team can write “help me feel confident” on a slide and call it research. The milkshake study’s discipline was observation plus interviews in the circumstance of purchase — who, when, with what constraints — not a brainstorm of emotional adjectives in a conference room. Without that fieldwork, “the job” is just a prettier persona.

Credit and method fights are public. Tony Ulwick and outcome-driven innovation claim earlier and more formal jobs-related tools; Bob Moesta appears in SNHU-adjacent accounts as a collaborator on interviews. This lesson teaches the Christensen HBR line because that is the named magazine trail (2005, 2016) and the book trail (2016). It does not settle who invented which worksheet.

Data systems push the other way. Christensen’s joke in the 2011 Working Knowledge piece is that God only made data available about the past, and that past data is filed by product category and customer category because those cuts are easy. Store shelves and org charts are often cut the same way. A tool that hangs a door in one step can still die if the retailer has no aisle for “hang a door.” Jobs theory names that friction; it does not erase it.

Overlap with Blue Ocean Strategy is real and partial. Both care about people the category has not been serving, and both warn against matching rivals on the industry’s usual list. Blue Ocean’s Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create grid rebuilds a value curve. Jobs theory asks what progress is being hired. You can use one without the other. You should not paste Cirque or the Wii into this lesson as if they were milkshake interviews.

sections.title: The book, the board seat, and the vocabulary that stuck

blocks.text: Competing Against Luck collected the argument in 2016. The Boston Globe excerpt the same October put SNHU in front of a general audience and noted Christensen’s past service on that university’s board — a relationship to disclose, not to hide. Product teams in software, especially, kept the hire/fire vocabulary; consultants multiplied canvases. Christensen died in 2020. The essays remain the public checkpoints.

What travels is the question order. Who is the buyer is still worth knowing. What progress are they hiring this for, in this circumstance, against which alternatives — that is the cut the 2005 essay said demographic dashboards were missing. When a team can answer it with observed constraints, not with invented poetry, the theory has done its job.
Pick one product you bought this week. What job did you hire it to do, what else were you considering, and which constraint (time, one hand, embarrassment, a child, a boss) decided it?
